Some commentators mistakenly argue that the meaning of ‘… and you, woman, plead for forgiveness for your sin’ is: ‘ask your husband not to punish you for your wrongdoing.’ They base this on the idea that the statement

comes from the witness and not from Potiphar. Another explanation is that it means: ‘Seek God’s forgiveness for your sin and repent to Him. The sin was yours, not Joseph’s.’ And this is because the Egyptians still believed in God Almighty even while they also worshipped idols.

Indeed, the idolaters acknowledged God in His role as the Creator, but they only worshipped deities and lords other than Him. This topic has been discussed earlier in our commentary. Note, however, that in the verse her husband only commands her: ‘plead for forgiveness for your sin’ without specifying from whom she should plead forgiveness, which in her faith would be whichever deity she worshipped.

Some have argued that the verse implies that Potiphar lacked jealousy, but the truth it points to is his deep love for his wife.

(12:30) Some of the townswomen (niswatun fī al-madīna) said, ‘The chieftain’s wife (imraʾat al-ʿazīz) solicits (turāwid) her slave boy (fatā-hā)! He has captivated her love (shaghafa-hā ḥubban).

Indeed we see her to be in manifest error.’

The verse initiates the story of the women of Egypt with Joseph in the house of Potiphar, which spans six verses.

Contemplating on these verses, keeping in mind the circumstances and the nature of the story, when the incident between Joseph and Potiphar’s wife took place, news of this gradually spread throughout the city. The women, who were the city’s elite, discussed it in their gatherings, taunting the wife of Potiphar, saying she was infatuated with the young man

and had been overtaken by love, persistently trying to seduce him. They believed she was in clear error. This was a cunning move on their part, typical of the envy and pride found in many women’s nature. A woman is often overwhelmed by delicate emotions and refined feelings. Her essence is adorned with beauty and grace, her heart captivated by allure. Such attributes, especially in young women, lead to conceitedness towards herself

and envy towards others.

In sum, their talk of love and temptation was a ruse aimed at the wife of Potiphar, providing them some solace and alleviating the resentment they felt in their hearts towards her. They had not seen Joseph as she had, nor had they witnessed what she did. They simply speculated and made assumptions. However, first-hand experience is distinct from mere storytelling, and first-hand observations differ from hearsay.

The gossip about Joseph eventually became so widespread that it reached the wife of Potiphar’s own ears. She, whose only concern was to have Joseph yield to her desires, cared little about her status or power; she only wished to make him love her in return. Recognizing the ladies’ scheme against her, she invited them to a soiree, knowing they were the elite and noble women of the city, connected socially to Potiphar’s household, and thus fit to be present at her gathering.

They prepared themselves, donning their most beautiful attire and ornaments, as was customary for such occasions among ladies of their rank. Each hoped to see Joseph and witness the charm that had so ensnared and exposed the wife of Potiphar. Her primary aim that day was to reveal them to Joseph so that they would understand her infatuation, thereby diverting their attention from her indiscretions. She felt secure in her position over him, deeming herself his mistress and owner. She believed he held no interest in other women, and she recognized his resistance to such temptations in any case.

Once they arrived and settled, the atmosphere became amiable. As they chatted and negotiated, each was given a knife, and fruits were presented before them. At that moment, she ordered Joseph to appear, who until then had been hidden from their view. The moment they set eyes on him, they were so taken aback and astonished that they accidentally cut their hands instead of the fruit. Such is the nature of intense surprise and shock: when one is pulled strongly towards something they deeply desire or fear, they can become disoriented. Sometimes, they may rush towards danger or, in their shock, become paralysed, acting without intention. Such cases related to passionate love are numerous, and the tales of the behavior of infatuated lovers are well-known.

This difference between the wife of Potiphar and the other women was evident. Her infatuation with Joseph developed gradually. In contrast, the women of the city were suddenly exposed to his beauty, and their hearts were overwhelmed all at once. This sudden surge of afiection disarmed them, disrupting their reason and discernment. They forgot about the fruit, inadvertently cutting their hands, discarding any restraint or patience. They outwardly displayed their intense love, exclaiming, ‘Good heavens! This is not a human being! This is but a noble angel!’

Furthermore, all of this occurred in the house of Potiphar, a place where utmost decorum and dignity were expected. They should have acted with caution and modesty. These women were noble, beautiful, and married, known for their modesty and chastity. All these factors should have restrained them from such open indiscretion. They hadn’t forgotten their recent discussions, where they criticized and condemned the wife of Potiphar for her infatuation with Joseph, even though they had been living under the same roof for years.

Each of them should have been more cautious than to indulge in such behavior. They knew well the scandal and the reputational damage the wife Potiphar had suffered because of Joseph. And Joseph stood before them, hearing their words and observing their actions.

However, the beauty of Joseph that they witnessed was so astonishing that it erased whatever opinions they had previously held. The setting, which should have been one of decorum and modesty, transformed into a vulgar celebration where attendees did not conceal their emotions or care about their appearance in front of others. Shortly after beholding him, they proclaimed, ‘Good heavens! This is not a human being! This is but a noble angel!’ While not long before that, they had whispered to one another, ‘The chieftain’s wife has solicited her slave boy! He has captivated her love. Indeed we see her to be in manifest error.’

The words they spoke upon beholding Joseph, after their initial criticism of Potiphar’s wife, served as a kind of confession. The essence of this

was that their earlier opprobrium of Potiphar’s wife would have been valid if Joseph were merely human. Humans can be blamed and criticized when they succumb to desires for another human, especially when they could find satisfaction in an equally attractive alternative. However, when faced with unmatched—no, supernatural—beauty that weakens one’s resolve and choice, one cannot be blamed for succumbing to its allure.

For this reason, the atmosphere of the gathering shifted abruptly. The bounds of modesty were broken as the women freely and openly discussed Joseph’s attractiveness. Each spoke according to her innermost feelings about him. The wife of Potiphar declared, ‘He is the one on whose account you blamed me. Certainly I did solicit him, but he was continent’ (12:32) She revealed a secret she had not previously admitted and threatened Joseph with imprisonment, both to maintain her status among the women of the city and in hope of securing his compliance, saying, ‘and if he does not do what I bid him, surely he shall be imprisoned and be among the abased.’ As for Joseph, he remained unafiected by the allure of these beautiful women, their captivating glances, their sweet talk, or the looming threat from the wife of Potiphar. Her turned fixed countenance upon the Beauty before which all other beauty fades and the Majesty before which all other might and dignity are abased. He neither engaged with them nor paid heed to the wife of Potiphar’s words. Instead, he turned to his Lord, praying, “‘My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me. If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them and become one of the senseless’ (12:33).

Comparing this plea to what he said to the wife of Potiphar during her initial seduction, ‘God forbid! Indeed He is my Lord; He has given me a good abode. Indeed the wrongdoers are not felicitous’, it becomes evident that the situation described in these verses was far more challenging for Joseph. Where once he resisted the advances of just the wife of Potiphar, now he faced the collective desires and intrigues of all the women of the town. The prior event occurred privately, with her attempting to conceal it. Yet now, these women openly professed their love, tempting him and conspiring to seduce him. The collective pressure exerted on him at this moment was significantly more intense than anything he had faced before. Therefore, Joseph fervently prayed to God to shield him from their plots. Previously, he merely sought God’s protection. In response, God answered his prayers, diverting their schemes from him. Truly, He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

Returning to the examination of the verses:

The term niswa refers to a group of women and, by mentioning they are fī al-madīna (‘in the city’), it indicates that they were either significant in number or influence, enough to spread the scandal widely.

Imraʾat al-ʿazīz (‘the chieftain’s wife’) is the one in whose house Joseph resided and who tried to seduce him. The title ʿazīz is well-known in Arabic, and it was the epithet used for the master who purchased Joseph from the caravan. This title was also used for dignitaries in Egypt, and later, Joseph himself was given this title when he was put in charge of the granaries of the land.

The word turāwid (‘solicits’) indicates continuity and intensifies the meaning of seduction (murāwada). The term fatā (‘slave boy’) usually denotes a young man but, in this context, it refers to a servant. So prevalent was the term for a servant that it was specifically attributed to her with the phrase ‘her slave boy.’

Regarding the phrase, shaghafa-hā ḥubban (‘he has captivated her love’), al-Rāghib writes in his M ufradāt:

‘According to al-Ḥasan, this implies that passion reached the innermost part of her heart. Or, according to Abū ʿAlī, the centre of

her heart— and these two meanings are similar.’

Different interpretations suggest it refers to the enveloping layer of the heart. Therefore, the meaning of the verse is as follows: ‘Several women of the city commented on the wife of Potiphar’s behavior, and their words were infiuential in the society. They pointed out that it is unseemly for a woman, especially a noblewoman like her, to try to seduce a man, let alone a servant. This behavior is generally expected of men, not women. As the wife of the chief, she should have been mindful of her household’s honor, her husband’s dignity, and her personal reputation. It is unbecoming of someone of her status to be infatuated with a foreign servant among her many servants. Her persistent attempts to seduce him, despite his refusals, were deemed reprehensible and a deviation from the path of good sense.’ Therefore, after saying, ‘The chieftain’s wife solicits her slave boy …’, they added: ‘Indeed we see her to be in manifest error.’

(12:31) When she heard of their machinations (makri-hinna), she sent for them and arranged a repast, and gave each of them a knife, and said, ‘Come out before them.’ So when they saw him, they marvelled at him and cut their hands, and they said, ‘Good heavens! This is not a human being! This is but a noble angel!’

In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī writes: ‘M akr (‘machinations’) refers to a cunning stratagem to covertly achieve one’s desires.’ Therefore, labelling their gossip as a makr against the wife of Potiphar reflects that they

intended to publicly shame her and diminish her dignity, and that, in this, they were motivated by jealousy and malice towards her. She summoned these women to display Joseph’s beauty to them and to put them to the test she faced, hoping they would then refrain from blaming her and understand her infatuation.

Given this context, their statements are labelled as cunning, and the wife of Potiphar is described as ‘hearing of’ them because these statements emanated from them out of envy and a desire to disgrace her among the people.

Some scholars have said that their statement is described as a makr because they used it as a pretext to meet Joseph, having heard of his extraordinary beauty. They uttered these words so that the wife of Potiphar would

hear and then invite them over, hoping to present Joseph before them. This would justify her infatuation with him and perhaps offer them an opportunity to also attempt to seduce him. However, the first explanation seems more consistent with the context of the verses.

The meaning of the phrase, she sent for them, is clear: It means that she invited them to assemble in her presence.

… and arranged a repast (aʿtaddat la-hunnā muttakaʾan), and gave each of them a knife—Aʿtaddat means that she made ready or set up, while muttakaʾ is the passive participle of the verb ittikāʾ (‘to recline’). Here, it denotes something one reclines against, like a cushion or a chair, especially as was custom in the houses of the elite. Some have understood this as a reference to citrus fruit (utruj). As for the phrase, and gave each of them a knife, this implies that he provided each of them with a knife to cut and eat the fruit laid out in front of them, such as citrus or other similar fruits. … and said, ‘Come out before them’—indicates that the wife of Potiphar ordered Joseph to appear before them. The phrasing here suggests that he had been kept out of their sight until this point, but that

he was somewhere in the house; perhaps in an adjoining room. Had he been outside the house, she would have said: ‘Enter upon them’ (idkhil ʿalay-hinna).

The narrative suggests that her soiree was a counter-strategy to the schemes of the womenfolk, to vindicate herself in their eyes. Her plan was well-executed: she prepared seating, gave each a knife, kept Joseph hidden, and then suddenly revealed him, hoping the shock of his striking beauty would catch them of  guard. The climax of this plan was their

accidental cutting of their hands, not just one or two of them, but all of them together.

So when they saw him, they marvelled at him and cut their hands, and they said, ‘Good heavens! This is not a human being! This is but a noble angel!’— This encapsulates their captivation and awe and symbolizes their astonishment and loss of self-control. Furthermore, it aligns with the universal principle that the lesser yields to the greater. W hen one encounters overwhelming beauty or grandeur, it dominates their senses, pushing

aside other thoughts and intentions, leading one to perform unintended acts.

Thus, when the women saw Joseph , the sight of him overwhelmed their senses, causing them to cut their own hands instead of the fruit they had intended to cut. The form of the verb qaṭṭaʿa (with emphasis on the middle radical, ṭ) indicates the repetitive or excessive nature of the action, much like saying, ‘The group was slaughtered ruthlessly’ (quttila) or ‘The drought killed them mercilessly’ (mawwata-hum— in both cases, there is an emphasis on the middle radical of the verb; t in quttila and w in mawwata). … they said, ‘Good heavens! (hāsha li llāh)—this is a glorification of God concerning the matter of Joseph. This is akin to another verse, ‘It is not for us to say such a thing. You are immaculate! This is a monstrous calumny!’ (24:16). It is a common style of speech amongst the eloquent that,

when speaking about a matter that pertains to someone’s exoneration or exaltation, they begin by magnifying and glorifying God, then proceed with what they wanted to say. Thus, when they wanted to exalt Joseph by saying, ‘This is not a human being!’they began by exalting God and then moved on to praising Joseph’s beauty.

In their statement, ‘This is not a human being! This is but a noble angel!’, they deny that Joseph could be a mortal man and declare him instead to be a blessed angel. This is based on the belief held by many, including the pagans, that angels are blessed beings, sources of all good and happiness in the world. From them emanates all life, knowledge, beauty, radiance, joy, and everything desirable. They embody both physical and moral beauty. W hen imagined, they are pictured as endowed with

unparalleled beauty, and those who worship idols often envisage them in handsome, appealing human forms.

Perhaps this is why they said, This is but a noble angel!’ They did not just describe him in terms of facial beauty or appealing appearance, even though what first afiected them was his indeed his outward presence. Instead, they called him a ‘noble angel,’ alluding to both his physical and moral beauty, and the beauty of his character and his appearance, both externally and internally.

The fact that this exclamation by the womenfolk comes before the wife of Potiphar said, ‘He is the one on whose account you blamed me’, indicates that they did not understand that their words excused her love for and infatuation with Joseph. On the contrary, their words were a spontaneous expression of admiration, an induced revelation of their own attraction to and infatuation with him. And this indeed exposed them, and the wife of Potiphar did not say, ‘He is the one on whose account you blamed me,’ until after they had unintentionally exposed themselves both through their deeds (cutting their hands) and through their words (praising his beauty). Therefore, they had no choice but to acknowledge the truth of her statement and to excuse her actions.

(12:32) She said, ‘He is the one on whose account you blamed me. Certainly I did solicit him, but he was continent, and if he does not do what I bid him, surely he shall be imprisoned and be among the abased.’

This verse appears to anticipate a question from the audience, namely: ‘What did Potiphar’s wife say to these women when this happened?’ She said, ‘He is the one on whose account you blamed me…’

Her response was based on the prior words and actions of her guests. She pointed to Joseph, the one for whom she had been blamed, depicting him as the very person responsible for her actions, the direct answer to their accusations of her having forsaken her household’s honor, her husband’s dignity, and her own chastity because of her infatuation with him.

The most powerful way to clarify an issue is to present the actual object of contention for all to see. A similar mode of expression can be found in the verses, ‘Is this the one who speaks ill of your gods?’ (21:36), and ‘Our Lord, it

was they who led us astray…!’ (7:38).

Subsequently, she confessed that she had attempted to seduce Joseph, informing the women that she did solicit him, but also that he held onto his virtue and sought God’s protection from such advances. She revealed to them what she had been concealing, especially when she saw their own hearts inclining towards him. She shared her frustrations with them, indicating to Joseph that she had not given up on him and that he should

prepare himself to obey her wishes. This sentiment is encapsulated in her statement, ‘Certainly I did solicit him, but he was continent …’

She then informed them of her determination to force Joseph into compliance with her wishes by outlining the consequences of his continued intractability. She stated, ‘and if he does not do what I bid him, surely he shall

be imprisoned and be among the abased (wa la-in lam yafʿal mā āmuru-hu la-yusjan-anna wa la-yakūnan min al-ṣāghirīn).’Note that her declaration is adorned with multiple linguistic devices, such as oaths and particles of emphasis (underlined above), to indicate her absolute determination. She implied that she possessed the means to force Joseph into compliance and that if he continued to disobey her, he should expect imprisonment after comfort and abasement after honor. Embedded within her words is a type of boastful warning directed towards the women who had previously gossiped about her, as well as a more direct threat to Joseph himself.

This threat, encapsulated in the passage, ‘and if he does not do what I bid him, surely he shall be imprisoned and be among the abased,’ is even more severe than what she presented to her husband on the day she tried to seduce Joseph, where she stated, “‘W hat is to be the requital of him who has evil intentions for your wife except imprisonment or a painful punishment?’ (12:25)

The distinction between the two threats lies in her earlier equivocation between imprisonment and severe punishment, while here she combines both consequences—namely imprisonment along with humiliation.

Secondly, here she made the threat herself, not by appealing to her husband. Her words are those of someone who is determined and unwavering

in their resolve. She demonstrated that she has control over her husband’s heart, capable of directing him from what he wants to what she desires. Can she exert control over his affairs as she pleases?

(12:33) He said, ‘My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me. If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline (aṣbu) towards them and become one of the senseless.’

Elaborating on the term aṣbu (‘incline’), al-Rāghib writes: ‘W hen someone inclines (ṣabā, yaṣbū, sabwā, and sibwa) they are driven by desire, as children (ṣibyān, which is derived from the same root) might be.’ In M ajmaʿ al-bayān, al-Ṭabrisī writes that ṣibwa refers to ‘the subtleties of desire.’

Potiphar’s wife and the womenfolk were engaged in a conversation.

They spoke together and elaborated their intentions, while Joseph stood before them as they tempted him. However, Joseph did not respond to them, nor did he address them, not even with a single word. Instead, he turned to his Lord, who possessed his heart entirely, with no room for anyone else and said, ‘My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me …’

Note that his statement is not a plea for imprisonment or for God to shield him from their temptations by sending him to jail. Instead, it’s a candid expression of his situation to his Lord. Due to his divine upbringing, he

considered the hardship of prison preferable to the pleasure of sinning and distancing himself from God. His words mirror what he told Potiphar’s wife when she was alone with him and tempted him, saying, ‘God forbid! Indeed He is my Lord; He has given me a good abode. Indeed the wrongdoers are not felicitous’ (12:23) In both statements, there’s a denunciation of sin and an affirmation of trust in God. The only difference is that in one, he addresses Potiphar’s wife, and in the other, he speaks to his powerful and mighty Lord. However, neither of these statements is a supplication per se. In his phrase, ‘M y Lord! The prison is dearer to me…’, he sets the stage for his subsequent words, ‘If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them …’ which takes the form of a supplication that is expressed as a statement of his situation.

The verse’s meaning is as follows: ‘My Lord, if I were to have to choose between going to prison and what they call me to do, I would prefer to go to prison. I ask You to protect me from their schemes. If You do not shield me from their plots, I might be drawn to them and become one of the ignorant. The only protection I seek from their evil is through the knowledge You have granted me. Without Your guidance, I would be lost, falling into the pitfalls of desire and passion.’

The context of the verse, aided by its surrounding narrative, makes the following points clear:

First of all, when Joseph says, ‘M y Lord! The prison is dearer to me …’ it is not a supplication by Joseph asking God to be imprisoned. Instead, it is a statement of his disposition, signifying his intention to turn away from the women attempting to seduce him and revert to God. The phrase ‘… dearer to me …’ means that he would prefer it over what they are trying to entice him towards, given the choice. This does not imply that he found their invitation enticing for its own sake but only insofar as it appealed to the inherent human nature and the low self (al-nafs al-ammāra) that often incites to evil.

Furthermore, the verse, ‘So his Lord answered him …’ (12:34) refers to the answer to his plea, specifically the part where he says, ‘If You do not turn away their schemes from me …’—this is further corroborated by the subsequent phrase, ‘… and turned away their stratagems from him.’ Therefore, this was not a response to his plea to be imprisoned, as some mistakenly believe.

Evidence for this can also be found later, in the account of his imprisonment, where it says, Then it appeared to them, after they had seen all the

signs, that they should confine him for some time (12:35). If Joseph had supplicated to God for imprisonment and God had decreed that for him, the

wording and meaning would not have been framed in this way.

Secondly, what is apparent is that these women, like the wife of Potiphar, attempted to seduce Joseph and lure him towards them. W hether these women invited him to themselves, or to the wife of the Potiphar, or both—where the nobleman’s wife invited him first, and then each woman privately tried to entice him— the verse remains silent. Yet, it can be inferred from his statement, ‘If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them …’ This suggests that if there weren’t invitations from each of them, the obvious meaning of his potential inclination

towards them would not make sense.

W hat substantiates this is the narrative of his conversation in prison with the king’s messenger: ‘Go back to your master, and ask him about the affair of women who cut their hands …’, continuing to where the wife of Potiphar confesses, ‘Now the truth has come to light! It was I who solicited him, and he is indeed telling the truth’… ‘that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not further the schemes of the treacherous’ (12:50-52). These verses suggest that these women invited him to the wife of Potiphar, and they were involved in the plot. Note that he says ‘I did not betray him in his absence’ (singular) and neither simply ‘I did not betray him’ or ‘I did not betray him and others.’ Reflect upon this. Nevertheless, it is highly improbable, given usual human behavior, that they witnessed something from him which astounded their senses and led them to cut their hands, only to then to leave him alone completely. More typically, having been so afiected, they would not have left that gathering without being deeply infatuated with him, consumed by thoughts of him day and night, willing to give anything and employ all means at their disposal to achieve their desires with him.

Therefore, it is apparent from what God has narrated about Joseph in His saying: ‘My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me. If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them …’, that Joseph did not turn from addressing the women to a private supplication to his Lord, who knows his condition and hears his speech, except due to the extreme adversity he faced and the overwhelming trial and calamity that beset him on their account.

Third, the divine strength with which Joseph was fortified was something gradually bestowed upon him time and again by God, the Most

Glorious. It was not something that was inherently present within him, or else there would have been no need for him to invoke God. That is why he expressed this as: ‘If You do not (present tense) turn away their schemes from me …’ rather than ‘If you had not turned (past continuous tense) their schemes from me …’ Even if the conditional statement is timeless, its conjugation has certain implications about time.

It is for this reason that God says, So his Lord answered him and turned away their stratagems from him. Here, the repelling of the evil from him is attributed to a new divine action of answering Joseph’s prayer and turning away the schemes of the womenfolk.

Fourth, this divine strength is in the realm of knowledge and thought. That is why Joseph said, ‘… and become one of the senseless (jāhilīn)’ not ‘I will become one of the wrongdoers (ẓālimīn)’, as he told the wife of Potiphar: Indeed the wrongdoers are not felicitous (12:23) or ‘I will become one of the treacherous (khāʾinīn)’, as he later tells the king: ‘Allah does not further the schemes of the treacherous’ (12:52). Note that there is a clear distinction in his address between them and his Lord. He addressed them concerning the outward aspect of the matter, on the basis of their level of understanding, by saying that it is a sin and wrongdoers are not felicitous, or it is an act of treachery and God does not guide the plots of the treacherous. Yet he addressed his Lord concerning the true nature of the matter,

which is that inclination towards them stems from ignorance.

The true nature of the situation concerning these two matters will be elaborated upon below, in a dedicated study on this topic.

(12:34) So his Lord answered him and turned away their stratagems from him. Indeed He is the All-hearing, the All-knowing.

This means that God responded to his plea to divert their schemes away from him when he said, ‘If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline towards them …’, and he explains this by invoking His divine names, the All-hearing and the All-knowing, to show that He is indeed the One who hears His servants speech and who is aware of their condition. An Excursus on Religious Piety and its Degrees 1. Law, Noble Ethics, and Monotheism:

Law can only flourish through a faith that is guarded by noble ethics, and noble ethics are complete only through monotheistic belief.

Monotheism is the root from which the tree of human happiness grows and branches into noble ethics. These branches produce good fruits in society. God says: Have you not regarded how Allah has drawn a parable? A good word is like a good tree: its roots are steady and its branches are in the sky. It gives its fruit every season by the leave of its Lord. Allah draws these parables for mankind so that they may take admonition. And the parable of a bad word is that of a bad tree: uprooted from the ground, it has

no stability (14:26). In this verse, God depicts faith in him as a tree with a root, which is unquestionably monotheism, and branches, which are noble characteristics such as piety, chastity, knowledge, courage, justice, mercy, and the like thereof.

God also says: To Him ascends the good word, and righteous conduct elevates it (35:10). In this verse, he associates the felicity of ascending toward

Him and closeness to Him with the good word, which is the true belief. The righteous deed that complements and enhances it is what elevates it in its ascent.

The explanation of this is as follows: It is evident that a person cannot achieve their potential nor find happiness in a life with no higher aim

than happiness itself unless they are part of a community that cooperates on the diverse tasks necessary for life. No single person can undertake all of these tasks alone.

This need for community is why humans must establish laws and regulations to protect the rights of individuals from negligence and corruption. Everyone can work to their fullest potential, and then they can

exchange their contributions with one another so that each receives an result proportional to their effort and its value to society, without the powerful oppressing the weak or the weak being exploited by the powerful. It is also a given that these laws and regulations will only be effective if they are backed by other punitive laws and measures. These laws threaten those who neglect their duties to society or infringe on the rights of others. They deter wrongdoers with consequences and, on the other hand,

encourage and inspire everyone to do good deeds. They also ensure that a governing power enforces these laws fairly and justly.

These aspirations can only be realized if the force that enforces the laws of society is aware of crime and sufficiently powerful to subdue the one who commits it. However, if this force remains ignorant, allowing transgressions to occur out of its own negligence or oversight—a not uncommon occurrence in human societies—then there is no impediment to corruption and disorder in society. Laws do not possess physical hands by which to enforce themselves. Similarly, if the government becomes weak due to a lack of necessary force or laxity in its policies and actions, and criminals overshadow its authority or even overpower it, the laws of society will lose their significance and violations against people’s rights become rampant. As has been discussed several times in earlier sections of this book, humans naturally lean toward benefiting themselves, even if they might harm others in the process.

This problem becomes more acute if such power is centralized in a single enforcing authority or a body that controls all affairs. This can weaken the populace, depriving them of the power to restore justice and rectify wrongs of their own accord. Such an entity becomes an uncontested and dominant force, whose power is unchallenged and whose will

is unquestioned.

Recorded histories are replete with tales of tyrants and oppressors and their unjust dominion over people. And this phenomenon is plainly visible throughout many parts of the world today.

While laws and norms may be just in their very essence, and while penal codes may be severe, they will not function efiectively in society nor close the door to crime and violations unless underpinned by virtuous human morals. Such morals should aim to eliminate oppression and corruption. This includes adhering to truth, respecting human dignity, advocating for justice, valuing life, and spreading compassion, among other noble traits. Do not be deceived by what you observe in advanced nations—the apparent strength, order, and justice. Even if their laws are not founded on ethical bases, these nations operate on a collective mindset. Their individuals prioritize the benefit and well-being of the nation as a whole, pushing

away anything that might harm their community. However, their primary concern for their own nation often translates into the exploitation of weaker nations, which is achieved through subjugating them, colonizing their lands, and violating their rights. This advancement and progress have merely shifted what past tyrants imposed on individuals to what presentday nations impose on other societies. The roles have changed: today’s

nation plays the role of yesterday’s individual. Meanings of terms have been distorted: words like freedom, honor, justice, and virtue are now invoked, but often they allude to their very opposites— slavery, degradation, injustice, and vice.

In summary, laws and norms cannot safeguard against violations and losses unless they are founded on and supported by noble human ethics. And morality or ethics, in its true essence, cannot bring happiness to society nor guide an individual toward righteous deeds unless it is anchored in the principle of monotheism. This principle is the belief that everything in the universe—including humankind—has one eternal God, from whom nothing is hidden. His power surpasses all creation, maintaining the most perfect order not out of need but because of His will. Eventually, He will summon all of His creation back to Him, rewarding the virtuous for their good deeds and punishing the wrongdoers for their transgressions. Based on their deeds, they will either enjoy eternal bliss or face perpetual torment. It is evident that when morality is grounded in this belief system, an individual’s primary concern becomes seeking God’s approval in all actions. Godwariness (taqwā), then, acts as an internal deterrent against wrongdoing. Without morals being nurtured by the monotheistic belief, an

individual’s sole purpose in life would devolve into seeking the ephemeral pleasures of this fieeting world and indulging in materialistic enjoyments. The utmost they could aspire to by adhering to societal rules and norms would be their own personal understanding that it is obligatory to abide by prevailing laws in order to prevent societal collapse or corruption. They might convince themselves that they should forsake some desires to sustain society, thereby gaining the residual benefits. People would then laud

and praise them during their lifetime, or history might remember them in positive term s.

However, public admiration and recognition typically only extend to significant deeds that come to light. As for smaller acts, especially those hidden from the public eye, there is no guarantee they will be shielded from criticism or malice. And when it comes to lasting recognition and lofty praise, this usually demands a great sacrifice, such as dying for one’s country, or investing time and money for the elevation of a nation, and such

things are seldom sought after. M oreover, any gains from these sacrifices after departing this worldly life are, from this perspective, based on mere superstitious beliefs. After all, according to this view of the world, there is no life after death, and thus, no possible benefit from any posthumous praise or recognition. Would any rational individual favor others’ joy by depriving themselves of their own without reaping any benefit as a result? Or would someone willingly choose death over life, if all they believe all that lies beyond this world is emptiness and nothingness? Superstitious beliefs tend to fade with the slightest awakening or reflection.

Certainly, it has become evident that such ideas cannot take the place of monotheism, nor can they deter a person from committing sins or violating norms and laws, especially when the action is naturally hidden from

the eyes of other people. This is especially so when it is in the nature of the action that, if revealed, it would appear contrary to its true nature due to certain circumstances. This is like the modesty, which is portrayed as an act of aggression or harm, as previously depicted in the story of Joseph when he was tempted by Potiphar’s wife. W hen he refused to betray Potiphar with his wife, he was falsely accused by her of trying to harm her. Nothing prevented him from doing this—and indeed nothing else is worthy of preventing him from doing this—save than the knowledge of his Lord’s station.

2. Religious piety is achieved through one of three ways:

Or, if you prefer, you might: God is worshipped through one of three paths: fear (khawf), hope (rajāʾ), and love (ḥubb). As stated in the Qurʾan

(57:20): Know that the life of this world is just play and diversion, and glitter, and mutual vainglory among you and covetousness for wealth and children— like the rain whose vegetation impresses the farmer; then it withers and you see it turn yellow, then it becomes chaff… Thus, a believer must recognize the reality of this world: It is but a fieeting illusion, like a mirage that

appears to be water to the thirsty. He must not make it the ultimate goal of his life’s deeds, knowing that beyond it is the hereafter, where the outcome of his actions resides: severe punishment for wrongdoings, which he must fear, and God’s forgiveness for righteous acts, which he should hope for, and God’s pleasure which should be placed above his own self-satisfaction. People differ in their inclination toward these three paths. The majority follow the path of fear, and every time they contemplate God’s promised punishment for oppressors and sinners, their fear intensifies, driving them to worship God out of fear of His punishment. Others are primarily driven by hope. Every time they think of God’s promise to the righteous—of blessings, honor, and a favorable outcome—their hope grows, and they increasingly practice piety and good deeds, desiring forgiveness and paradise.

A third group, the ones who truly know God, do not worship Him out of fear of punishment or in anticipation of a reward. They worship Him because He is worthy of worship. They know Him through attributes and names that befit His greatness, understanding that He is their Lord, controlling their existence, desires, contentment, and everything else, and that He alone governs all the affairs of reality. They see themselves as mere servants of His, and a servant’s duty is to worship his Lord, prioritizing His wishes and desires over his own. They worship God, seeking His countenance in all their actions, whether through performance or abstention, without being distracted by fear of punishment or hope of reward.

Even if they fear His punishment and hope for His mercy, this sentiment is reflected in the saying: ‘I did not worship You out of fear of Your Hell, or for the desire of Your Paradise. Rather, I found You worthy of worship, so I worshipped You.’

When people subsume their own desires and wants in order to pursue the pleasure of their Lord and dedicate their actions toward seeking their ultimate goal, which is God, a divine love will blossom in their hearts. This love stems from recognizing God through the ways He has made Himself known to them. He has identified Himself using the most beautiful names and described His essence with every attribute of perfection. It is innate to human nature to be drawn to beauty; thus, how could one not be attracted to Absolute Beauty? God proclaimed, That is Allah, your Lord, there is no god except Him, the creator of all things; so worship Him (6:102). He also said, who perfected everything that He created (32:7). These verses suggest that creation itself revolves around beauty, and that beauty and creation are inseparable. Moreover, God often reminds us through various verses that everything He created is a sign pointing to Him. Indeed, in the heavens and the earth are signs for those of understanding. There is nothing

in existence that does not point to His presence or convey something of His beauty and majesty.

From the perspective of their creation and inherent beauty, all things point toward His endless beauty, proclaiming His praises and lauding His everlasting magnificence. Conversely, from the viewpoint of their limitations and needs, all things point to His absolute sufficiency, revering and

glorifying His sanctity and grandeur. As God said, There is not a thing but celebrates H is praise (17:44).

These individuals pursue an understanding of things by following the path that God has guided them to, recognizing these things as signs and indicators of His own beauty and majesty. These signs, in their essence and origin, merely reflect the infinite beauty that lies beyond, highlighting their own neediness and the encompassing nature of God’s complete sufficiency, and the humility and dependence that contrasts with His supreme power and grandeur. One who reflects upon the universe from this perspective will inevitably feel an overwhelming attraction to the realm of divine greatness, with their heart immersed in spiritual love to such an extent that they

forget themselves and everything else. Such a gaze purifies the soul, erasing personal desires and whims, replacing one’s innermost being with a heart that is entirely devoted to God, as God mentioned, but the faithful have a more ardent love for Allah (2:165).

Hence, those who follow this spiritual path believe that the other two paths—worshipping God out of fear or worshipping Him in anticipation of rewards— are not truly free from associating partners with Him. Those who worship Him out of fear of His punishment are essentially seeking His protection from that punishment, just as those who worship Him in hope of rewards seek His favor and honor, but not God Himself. In other words, if they could attain their desires without worshipping Him, they would not bother seeking knowledge of Him. As has been narrated from al-Ṣādiq: ‘Is religion (dīn) anything other than love (ḥubb)?’ And he also said in a tradition, ‘Indeed, I worship Him out of love for Him, and this is a hidden station that can only be reached by the purified.’ The true lovers of God are purified because they are devoid of self sh desires and materialistic tendencies. True sincerity in worship is only achieved through the

path of love.

3. How does love inspire devotion (ikhlāṣ)?

Worshipping God out of fear of punishment motivates a person toward renunciation (zuhd), which is the practice asceticism in worldly matters in order to secure salvation in the hereafter. An ascetic tends to avoid prohibited actions or anything akin to them—meaning neglecting obligatory duties. On the other hand, worshipping God in hope of reward prompts one toward action, which is worshipping in this world through righteous deeds to attain blessings in the afterlife and paradise. Such a worshipper is inclined to fulfill obligatory duties or anything resembling them,

i.e., refraining from the forbidden. Both these paths lead one to devotion to the religion, not to the Lord of the religion.

As for the love of God, it purifies the heart from attachments to anything other than Him, be it worldly allurements or its adornments, one’s

children, one’s spouse, wealth, prestige, even one’s own self with all its aspirations and desires. This love restricts one’s heart to connect only with God and what is attributed to Him, be it a religion, a prophet, a saint, and everything that traces back to Him— because when you love someone, you naturally love everything associated with them.

Thus, a person who possesses this love prefers actions that are beloved to God and detests those that God disapproves of. He feels content with what pleases God and feels angered by what angers God. This love becomes the light illuminating their path of action. As God says, … he who was lifeless, then We gave him life and provided him with a light by which he walks

among the people … (6:122). It becomes the spirit guiding them toward good deeds and righteous actions, as God says, He has written faith into their hearts and strengthened them with a spirit from Him (58:22). The secret lies in the fact that only good and beauty emanate from such a person, and they avoid everything despicable and evil.

Regarding the observable universe and the events that unfold therein, when such a person gazes upon anything, be it significant or trivial, abundant or sparse, they cherish and appreciate it. This is because they perceive

everything as pure signs that reveal, beyond their immediate appearance, an embodiment of absolute beauty and unparalleled charm, devoid of any fiaws or aversion.

For this reason, such an individual is enveloped in God’s blessings, experiencing joy without sorrow, pleasure without pain, and security without fear. Such negative feelings arise from beholding evil or anticipating

harm. Those who see only goodness and beauty, and feel only what aligns with God’s desires and contentment, are beyond sorrow, pain, or fear. Only God can grasp the extent of their sense of joy, security, and elation. Such matters are often too profound for ordinary souls to fathom, except through an imperfect mode of understanding.

This reality is alluded to in verses such as: Look! The friends of Allah will indeed have no fear nor will they grieve. Those who have faith, and are Godwary (10:62–3), and Those who have faith and do not taint their faith with wrongdoing—for such there shall be safety, and they are the rightly guided (6:82).

These are the individuals who are closest to God, having nothing obstructing their connection to Him, be it physical senses, illusions, personal whims, or satanic insinuations. Everything they perceive is a sign

revealing the divine truth without any veil. They are endowed with the knowledge of certitude (ʿilm al-yaqīn). God unveils hidden realities beyond the comprehension of the physical eyes. This is indicated in verses like: No indeed! The record of the pious is indeed in Illiyun. And what will show you what is Illiyun? It is a written record, witnessed by those brought near (83:18- 21), and “ No indeed! W ere you to know with the knowledge of certitude, you would surely see hell (102:5–6). Previous discussions on this topic can be found in our commentary on the verse, O you who have faith! Take care of your own souls (5:105).

In summary, these individuals truly rely on God, place their trust in Him, are content with His decree, and submit fully to His will. They see only His goodness and beauty in all things, and hence their souls are imbued with noble qualities and virtues in line with this high level of monotheism. They are as devoted to God in their ethical values just as they are in their deeds. This is the essence of dedicating one’s religion purely to God, as He has stated: He is the Living One, there is no god except Him. So supplicate Him, putting exclusive faith in Him (40:65).

4. God’s devotion (ikhlāṣ) toward His servant:

This refers to what the servant finds within himself as devotion, which he then attributes to God. Indeed, the servant possesses nothing of himself except through God. God, in His majesty, is the owner of whatever spiritual blessings He grants the servant. Even devotion in one’s faith— or, if you prefer, say: one’s devotion toward God—is an act of divine grace by which God endows a person with that devotion toward Himself.

Indeed, here is a point to consider: God, in all His glory, created some of His servants with an upright nature and balanced temperament. They emerged from the beginning with sound minds, proper understanding, pure souls, and wholesome hearts. Due to their innate purity and integrity of soul, they acquired a level of devotion and sincerity that others might only achieve through effort and striving, yet even more profound and elevated due to their internal purity from the contamination of impediments and distractions. It appears that these individuals are the ones who

are the mukhlaṣūn (‘exclusive servants’) to God as understood in the context of the Qurʾan.

And these individuals are the prophets and the imāms. The Qurʾan explicitly states that God chose them, meaning that He gathered them for Himself and purified them for His presence. God says, We chose them and guided them to a straight path. (6:87) and He has chosen you and has not placed for you any obstacle in the religion (22:78).

God endowed them with knowledge that serves as a shield against them committing sins or transgressions. Endowed with this knowledge, they abstain from every sin, whether minor or major. This characteristic distinguishes infallibility (ʿiṣma) from moral rectitude or righteousness (ʿadāla). W hile both prevent sinful actions, infallibility inherently prevents the contemplation of sins, unlike moral rectitude.

It has been established that a unique attribute of these special individuals is that they possess knowledge from their Lord that others do not. God affirms this when He says, Clear is Allah of whatever they allege, except Allah’s exclusive servants (37:160). The divine love inspires them to desire only what God desires, and thus they refrain from all kinds of transgressions. God reinforces this point with His account of Satan, saying, He

said, ‘By Your might, I will surely pervert them, except Your exclusive servants among them’ (Sad: 83).

Evidence that infallibility is related to knowledge can be found in God’s words addressing His Prophet, Were it not for Allah’s grace and His mercy on you, a group of them were bent on leading you astray; but they do not mislead anyone except themselves, and they cannot do you any harm. Allah has

sent down to you the Book and wisdom, and He has taught you what you did not know, and great is Allah’s grace upon you (4:113). We have elaborated on the meaning of this verse in our commentary on Sūrat al-Nisāʾ.

Further, God recounts the words of Joseph, He said, ‘My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me. If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline toward them and become one of the senseless’ (12:33). We have explained how this verse points to this concept, above. From this, it is evident that this knowledge differs from other types in its practical impact. It decisively and consistently guides human beings away from what is inappropriate and toward what is appropriate, unlike other forms of knowledge, which might influence people in this manner probabilistically but not always decisively. God says, They impugned

them—though they were convinced in their hearts—wrongfully and defiantly

(27:14), Have you seen him who has taken his desire to be his god and whom Allah has led astray knowingly (45:23), and But they did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves (45:17). Further evidence for this can be found in the verse: Clear is Allah of whatever they allege, except Allah’s exclusive servants (37:160). These exclusive servants from the ranks of the Prophets and Imāms have clarified for us

the sum of knowledge related to His exalted names and attributes through revelation. We have also attained this knowledge through rational proofs. Yet, the verse emphasizes God’s transcendence beyond any description we might give Him, except for those descriptions provided by these devoted servants. Thus, one form of knowledge does not equate to another, even if they both pertain to the same subject.

Secondly, this knowledge (ʿilm)— referring to the grace of infallibility (ʿiṣma)—does not alter the human being’s inherent nature in his voluntary actions nor does it push him into the realm of compulsion and predestination. How is this? Knowledge is fundamentally a product of choice,

and merely possessing knowledge does not necessitate a strong will. For instance, if someone who cares to preserve his own wellbeing is certain that a liquid is a lethal poison, they will undoubtedly avoid drinking it of their own free will. An actor is only compelled when they are forced to choose one of two equally possible options, leading to one becoming impossible for them.

Evidence for this includes the verse: We chose them and guided them to a straight path. That is Allah’s guidance: with it He guides whomever He wishes of His servants. But were they to ascribe any partners (to Allah), what they used to do would not avail them (6:88). This verse implies that they still have the capability to associate partners with God, even though divine selection and guidance prevent them from doing so. Another verse states: O M essenger! Communicate that which has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, you will not have communicated His message (5:67), among other verses.

The infallible human refrains from committing sins by their own accord, choice, and free will. This aversion to sin due to their infallibility is analogous to the divine favor that ordinary individuals receive to assist them in abstaining from sins.

Furthermore, this does not contradict what is indicated in God’s words and explicitly mentioned in traditions, namely that Prophets and Imāms are divinely guided by the Holy Spirit (rūh al-qudus). Relating to the Holy Spirit is like attributing the guidance of a believer to the spirit of faith and attributing a person’s misguidance to the influence of the devil. Nevertheless, none of this removes the act from being a result of the actor’s choice and will. Understand this well.

There are some theologians who claim that God only diverts a person from sin not through their own choice and volition but by intervening in the natural causes, imbuing them with a will, sending an angel to resist a person’s will, preventing its influence, or diverting it from its natural course. This is like a strong person preventing a weaker one from doing something that is in their nature to do.

Some of these scholars, even though they incline toward determinism, share a common foundation with one another, upon which they base their worldview. They believe that things require God, the True Creator, only in their inception. Once these things come into existence, they no longer need Him. He, in His transcendence, plays a role in the sequence of causality. However, being the most powerful and dominant over all, He has

the authority to intervene in matters of existence, whether to prevent or permit, give life or cause death, heal or inflict illness, grant abundance or restrict, and so forth, by His supreme power.

If God desires to divert a servant from evil, for instance, He might send an angel to challenge the individual’s natural inclinations, altering their will from evil to good. Conversely, if God wishes to mislead a servant due to their deserving of such a fate, He might allow Satan to influence them, turning them from good to evil, but not in a manner that necessitates complete compulsion.

This view is countered by our own direct experiences of reality as human beings. When we observe our own actions, whether these are good or evil, it is evident that there isn’t any external force contending with us or threatening to overpower us beyond our own selves. We perform our actions based on our feelings and a choice that emerges from these feelings. Thus, whatever is established by our senses and reason concerning

external influences on our souls, such as angels or devils, is a longitudinal cause and not a transversal one, and this is clear.

Furthermore, the Qurʾanic teachings on monotheism and its attendant doctrines refutes this viewpoint at its core. A substantial portion of this has already been examined in earlier discussions.

Examining Narrations

(1) Shaykh al-Ṣadūq reports in Maʿānī al-Akhbār from Abū Ḥamza al-Thumālī from Imām al-Sajjād, in a narration that we already began to examine in the previous section:

‘Joseph was among the most beautiful people of his time. When Joseph reached adolescence, the wife of the king sought to seduce him, but he said, “God forbid, we, the people of the house, do not commit adultery.” She locked the doors and said, “Do not be afraid!” Then she threw herself at him. Joseph escaped and ran toward the door. She chased him and pulled his shirt from behind, tearing it of . Joseph escaped from her in his clothes. W hen they encountered her husband at the door, she said, “What is the punishment for someone who intended harm to your household?

Shouldn’t it be imprisonment or a painful punishment?”

The king intended to punish Joseph, but Joseph said, “I didn’t intend any harm to your household. She sought to seduce me.

Just ask this young boy who had tried to seduce the other. God made the boy speak to resolve the matter. He said, “O King, look at Joseph’s shirt. If it is torn from the front, he is the one who seduced her, and if it is torn from the back, she is the one who seduced him.”

When the king heard the boy’s words, he was greatly alarmed.

He looked at the shirt, and when he saw it torn from the back, he said to her, “This is from your guile! Your guile is great indeed!” He told Joseph: “Let this matter alone and not to let anyone hear about it from you.” However, Joseph did not keep it a secret and spread it throughout the city. The women of the city began to say, “The chieftain’s wife solicits her slave boy!” W hen she heard this, she invited them, prepared food for them, and gave each of them a knife. Then she told Joseph to come out to them. When they saw him, they praised him and cut their hands. The women left, and each of them secretly sent a message to Joseph, asking to visit him. He refused and said, “ If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline toward them and become one of the senseless.” But God turned away their plot.

When the matter of Joseph, the nobleman’s wife, and the women became known in Egypt, the king decided to imprison Joseph after hearing the boy’s words. So, he was put in prison. Two young men were imprisoned with Joseph, and their story and Joseph’s story is what God has narrated in the Qurʾan.’ Abū Ḥamza said, ‘Then the narration of ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn ended.’

Author’s comment: In his Tafsīr, al-ʿAyyāshī narrates a tradition with the same meaning from Abū Ḥamza with slight differences. In his version, “God forbid, we, the people of the house, do not commit adultery” is an explanatory gloss which is inserted beside verse, Indeed He is my Lord; He has given me a good abode (12:23). This supports what we have said regarding the verse, namely that the pronoun refers to God, not to Potiphar, as

most commentators have suggested. Understand this.

Furthermore, when the Imām says, ‘He refused and said, “If you do not turn away …”’, this shows that he did not consider Joseph’s statement, ‘My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me’ (12:33) a kind of supplication, which is also consistent with what we have previously said about the verse.

(2) In ʿUyūn Akhbār al-Riḍā, it is reported from Ḥamdān, from ʿAlī b. Muḥammad b. al-Jahm: ‘I attended a salon (majlis) of the Caliph al-Maʾmūn and with him was ʿAlī b. Mūsā al-Riḍā.

Al-Maʾmūn said to him, “O son of the Messenger of God, do you not assert that the prophets are infallible?” He said, “Yes.” Then the discussion continued until the Caliph said, “Then inform me about the meaning of God’s saying, She certainly made for him;

and he would have made for her had he not beheld the proof of his Lord.” Al-Riḍā said: “She certainly made for him, and had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have certainly made for her, but he was infallible, and the infallible neither intends to commit a sin nor does he commit one.”

Surely my father told me from his father al-Ṣādiq that he said, “She made to do it, and he made not to do it.” Al-Ma’mun said, “May God bless you, O Abū al-Ḥasan!”’

Author’s comment: We have previously mentioned that this Ibn alJahm is not without issue when it comes to the reliability of his narrations. However, what al-Riḍā says at the beginning of the narration is consistent with what we have previously explained with regards to this verse. As for what he narrated from his grandfather Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq, ‘She made to do it, and he made not to do it,’ perhaps the intended meaning is what Imām al-Riḍā had already mentioned, and this is an example of him applying this tradition to it. Or perhaps the intended meaning is that he made to kill her, as the following narration supports, which is consistent with some of the previous possible explanations of the verse.

(3) In ʿUyūn Akhbār al-Riḍā, it is reported from Abū al-Ṣilt al-Harawī, who said: ‘When the Caliph al-Maʾmūn gathered for ʿAlī b. Mūsā al-Riḍā the people of different theological schools from among the M uslims, and from representatives of different religions, including Jews, Christians, Magians, Sabians, and all the people who

espoused different doctrines, no one stood up except that ʿAlī b.

M ūsā had soundly defeated his argument, and the representative stood there dumbfounded, as if he had fed him a stone.

ʿAlī b. Muḥammad b. al-Jahm stood up to him and said, “O son of the Messenger of God, do you say that the prophets are infallible?” He said, “Yes.” He said to him, “So what do you say about

His saying about Joseph, She certainly made for him; and he would have made for her?” ʿAlī al-Riḍā said to him, “As for His saying, the Exalted, about Joseph, She certainly made for him; and he would have made for her had he not beheld the proof of his Lord, she intended to commit a sin, but Joseph intended to kill her if she forced him to do what she wanted him to do. So, God turned away from him killing her and from immorality. This is His saying, the Mighty and Majestic, So it was, that We might turn away from him all evil and indecency. He was indeed one of Our dedicated servants. And evil refers to killing, while indecency is adultery.”’ (4) In al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī reports from Abū Naʿīm, who reported in his Hilya from ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib about the verse, She certainly made for him; and he would have made for her: ‘She desired him, and he desired her, and his desire was that he intended to unbuckle his belt. So, she went to an idol adorned with pearls and rubies in a corner of the house. She covered it with a white cloth between her and it. He asked, “What are you doing?” She said, “I am ashamed before my god to see me in this state.” So, Joseph said, “You are ashamed of an idol that does not eat or drink, and I am not ashamed before my God, who is aware of every soul for what it has earned?” Then he said, “You will never get it from me.” And this is the proof that he saw.’

Author’s comment: This narration is fabricated. How can it be otherwise? The speech of Imām ʿAlī and of all of the Imāms of the Prophet’s

Household is replete with discussions about the infallibility of the prophets, and their doctrine in this regard is well known.

M oreover, her covering the idol, his reaction to this, and the argument he made to her is not called beholding the proof of his Lord. This idea has been mentioned in several narrations from the Prophet’s Household, but these are solitary reports and, as such, they cannot be relied upon. Yes, it is not unlikely that the woman would go to cover an idol that was there, so Joseph’s self would be drawn to witnessing the signs of monotheism at that, so the veil between him and the field of divine majesty would be lifted, and he would see what would turn him away from all evil and immorality, as he had before. And God has said about him, He was indeed one of Our dedicated servants. If anything from these narrations is correct, let this be its meaning.

(5) In al-Durr al-manthūr, Abū al-Shaykh reports from Ibn ʿAbbās:

‘Joseph stumbled three times: when he made for her, so he was imprisoned; when he said, “Mention me to your master”, so he stayed in prison for several years, and Satan made him forget the remembrance of his Lord; And when he said, “You are indeed thieves!” (12:70), they said “If he has stolen; a brother of his had stolen before” (12:77).

Author’s comment: This narration contradicts the explicit words of God, where He mentions that He chose him and made him exclusively for Himself, and that Satan has no way to those whom God has made exclusively for Himself. How can it be correct for someone who intended the worst sin, and Satan made him forget the mention of his Lord, then he lied in his statement so God punished him with prison, then with staying in it for several years, and accused him of theft, that God would consider him a truthful one of His chosen and beneficent servants, and mention that He gave him authority and knowledge, chose him, and completed His favor upon him? There are many weak narrations of this kind that al-Suyūṭī has reported in al-Durr Al-Manthūr, and some of them have been previously transmitted when clarifying the verses— nothing from them can be relied upon.

(6) In al-Durr al-manthūr, al-Suyūṭī cites Aḥmad, Ibn Jarīr, and al-Bayhaqī’s Dalāʾil, who report from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (s.a.w.): ‘Four spoke while they were infants: the son of M āshiṭa the Pharaoh’s daughter, Joseph’s witness, the companion of the wounded one, and Jesus son of Mary.’

(7) In the Tafsīr of al-Qummī, he narrates from Abū al-Jārūd from Abū Jaʿfar, about the verse: He has captivated her love: ‘Her love for him veiled her from the people, so she did not understand anything other than him, and the veil is passion, and passion is the veil of the heart.’

(8) In the same source, in a narration about the gathering of the women and their cutting their hands, he said: ‘Joseph did not end that day until every woman who saw him sent a message to him, inviting him to come to her. Joseph was annoyed that day and said, “My Lord! The prison is dearer to me than to what they invite me. If You do not turn away their schemes from me, then I will incline toward them and become one of the senseless” (12:33). Therefore, his Lord responded to him and turned away from him their plot.’
